(Marijuananews note: Please note correction on source. This was not from the Washington Post. They don't have a monopoly on reefer madness, just a few improvement patents. My apologies, even to the Post.)
From San Luis Obispo County Tribune
http://www.thetribunenews.com/
By Dr. Peter Gott wgroshong@Thetribunenews.com

THE MEDICINAL QUALITIES OF MARIJUANA

Dear Dr. Gott: I have been using marijuana to overcome the unpleasant consequences of chemotherapy for cancer.

Am I running any health risks?

Dear Reader: Although authorities estimate that over 50 percent of people will illegally use marijuana sometime in their lives, many medical experts endorse the use of the drug - or its active ingredient, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol - for cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy.
(Marijuananews note: The opening clause is irrelevant to the second. If half of the population will use marijuana illegally, what bearing does that have on whether a doctor would endorse its medical use?)

Unfortunately this practice is, at the time of this writing, against the law, except when THC is physician-prescribed.

The effects of marijuana last up to three hours and include, euphoria, heightened sensations and increased sexual arousal.
(Marijuananews note: Someone undergoing cancer chemotherapy is going to experience " increased sexual arousal? " In fact, that is not the effect experienced by most users that I know, dammit.)

On the other hand, between 40 and 60 percent of marijuana-users report unpleasant side effects. THC accumulates in fatty tissues and can lead to reduced size of testicles, low testosterone levels, menstrual irregularity, impotence, infertility, fetal damage (in pregnant women), (Marijuananews note: Virtually all of this is crap. There is not the slightest evidence of " fetal damage " from marijuana use. The only reported drop in testosterone levels was within the normal range and there has been no study of testicle size.)
See
Fetal Alcohol Syndrome:
Media Reports Decry Effects Of Illegal Drugs Such As Marijuana, Cocaine And Heroin.
" They don’t have anywhere near the effect that alcohol does on the unborn baby. "
prolonged childbirth and reduced sexual urge.
(Marijuananews note: Excuse me, but didn’t he just say that it " increased sexual arousal? Also, marijuana has been used to ease child-birth for centuries.)

Other common consequences

of the substance are: dry mouth, nausea, headache, tremor, rapid pulse, reduced muscle strength, decreased brain blood-flow, increased appetite, anxiety, confusion, paranoia, hallucinations, sedation, poor sense of self and time, shortened memory, addictive behaviors, and lack of motivation.
(Marijuananews note: Some of these effects, such as dry-mouth, sedation, and increased appetite are indeed common, and even desirable, others are rare, transitory or non-existent. Most are irrelevant to a medical user.)

Moreover, THC is known to cause decreased coordination, lung damage, increased risk of infection, heart problems and cognitive defects.
(Marijuananews note: With the partial exception of some decreased coordination at the time of acute intoxication, i.e. being very stoned, none of these effects are attributed to THC by the FDA in its approved drug Marinol, which is what he then goes on to recommend.)
See
Marinol Was The First Schedule 2 Drug To Be " Down-Scheduled, "
Boasts Roxanne On Its New Marinol.com Web Site.
Doesn’t That Mean That It Should Never Have Been Schedule 2 Anyway?
Obviously, the social use of marijuana can be fraught with problems.
(Marijuananews note: That is not the question.)
In addition, the metabolic products of the drug can be detected in the urine by routine screening for months after use. I believe that recreational use of marijuana, therefore, is risky.
(Marijuananews note: Again, that is irrelevant to the question about medical use, especially for someone undergoing chemotherapy whose use will be very occasional over a relatively short period of time. Also, how do all of the above alleged side-effects compare with those of other drugs commonly given to cancer patients, including morphine?)
In contrast, THC for cancer patients seems to be reasonable. The potential benefits, such as relief of nausea and a feeling of improved well-being, far out-weigh the possible health risks.

I see no reason why you shouldn't use THC to ameliorate the consequences of chemotherapy.
(Marijuananews note: Presumably he has never seen anyone vomit, which – considering his medical advice – is a minor miracle. This incoherent mishmash leaves the patient afraid to take THC in marijuana, but the reason for smoking is simply for its rapid onset, ease of titration, and the fact that the other cannabinoids, which Gott seems never to have heard of, reduce the side-effects of pure THC. No one, least of all the patient, has been well-served by this, except the prohibitionist party line.)
See
Counterblaste to DEA: Fallacious Pharmacology.
" The contention that smoking cannot possibly be an acceptable route for the administration
of a therapeutic substance is morality dressed up as science. " by Peter Webster
